tagline: Query relational data in SQL, predict the result before you run it, and prove the answer right against a known one
description: Participants query relational data in SQL and check that the answers are right. In an embedded analytical engine on a laptop they move from keys and constraints through joins, grouping and common table expressions to window functions. They predict results before running queries, catch the silent errors that joins and NULLs cause, and test assistant-written SQL against known answers. The capstone answers a stakeholder brief on an unseen dataset.
audience: Beginners. Anyone starting technical data or AI work, including future analysts, data scientists, data engineers and AI engineers who can code but have not yet worked with messy real data.
prerequisites: Comfortable with spreadsheets: filters, sorting and simple formulas

outcomes.text: Explain the relational model: tables, keys, constraints, NULL and the grain of a table, given a six-table synthetic delivery schema
outcomes.evidence: an annotated schema with keys, cardinalities and grain matching the reference

outcomes.text: Identify the output of joins, grouping and NULL comparisons before running them, given small printed tables
outcomes.evidence: supervised AI-off check, eight of ten correct

outcomes.text: Write queries with filters, joins, grouping, subqueries and common table expressions that answer business questions, given a synthetic dataset of about a million order lines
outcomes.evidence: a query file passing the automatic checker on 16 of 20 questions

outcomes.text: Apply window functions to rank rows, compare periods and compute running and moving totals, given daily order tables
outcomes.evidence: queries matching reference outputs, each partition explained in a comment

outcomes.text: Implement a small schema with keys and constraints, load raw files into it and report rejected rows, given extracts with seeded defects
outcomes.evidence: a definition script and a load log accounting for every rejected row

outcomes.text: Identify silent errors in assistant-written SQL, such as join fan-out, wrong grain and missing business rules, given ten generated queries and a revenue rule documented outside the schema
outcomes.evidence: a verification note judging each query, with a test result

case_study.name: The grocery delivery company
case_study.summary: An online grocery and household goods delivery business in one city of five regions, dispatching from eight stores; every lab works on its synthetic six-table schema of about a million order lines from January to June 2026, with planted traps: delivery attempts that multiply rows, discounts left NULL, cancelled lines, closed days and a revenue rule finance keeps outside the schema. The capstone uses an unseen dataset from the company's business orders service; all data is synthetic and people appear only as roles and codes.

format_note: Intensive: 4 teaching days and a capstone day, with guided pre-work and a tracked follow-up task

days.title: Tables, keys and grain

sessions.title: Tables, types, keys and constraints
sessions.summary: A table is a set of rows of one kind; keys name a row, constraints refuse a bad one
outcomes: Name the type and the role of each column of a table
Test a candidate key with a counting query
Read the message a database gives when a constraint refuses a row

lab.title: Six tables and their keys
lab.summary: List the six tables of the grocery delivery company, read their columns and types, test each candidate key by counting, and watch a key and a check refuse bad rows

steps.text: List the six tables with their row counts
Describe the columns and types of each table
Test each candidate key: COUNT(*) against COUNT(DISTINCT key)
Break a key and a check on the mini tables and read the refusals
Write down what each table refuses and why

lab.stretch: Find one column whose type is weaker than its meaning and say what that lets in

sessions.title: Grain and cardinality
sessions.summary: What one row stands for, and how many rows of one table meet one row of another
outcomes: State the grain of a table in one sentence
Confirm a grain with a counting query
Measure a one-to-many relationship and name its maximum

lab.title: The annotated schema
lab.summary: Write the key and the grain of each of the six tables, confirm them with counting queries, measure the cardinality of every relationship and check the annotated schema against the reference

steps.text: Write the grain of each table in one sentence
Confirm each grain with a counting query
Measure lines per order, attempts per order and orders per customer
Fill in the annotated schema and run its check

lab.stretch: List every join of the schema that can multiply rows, and the column that causes it

sessions.title: Normal forms, wide tables and embedded engines
sessions.summary: Why operational tables are split, why analytical tables are wide, and where the engine runs
outcomes: Explain the repetition that normal forms remove
Build a wide analytical table from a join and name its risks
Contrast an embedded engine with a client-server database

lab.title: One wide table, and what it repeats
lab.summary: Join order lines to their order, store and product into one wide table, count what it repeats, make one copy disagree, and run the same count in a second embedded engine

steps.text: Build a wide table of order lines with store and product columns
Count how often each store's region is repeated
Change one region in the wide table and find the rows that now disagree
Run the same count in the second embedded engine

lab.stretch: Write two sentences on when the wide table is the right choice and who must rebuild it

sessions.title: Filters, sorting and expressions
sessions.summary: WHERE on text and dates, ORDER BY with ties, and expressions that compute a value per row
outcomes: Filter rows on text patterns and date ranges
Sort with a tie-breaker and keep the top rows
Compute a value per row with an expression that handles a NULL

lab.title: Questions 1 to 4, predicted first
lab.summary: Write a prediction, then the query, for the first four of the twenty business questions: text filters, a date range, a sorted top ten and a line value; save them to your answer file

steps.text: Read the four questions and write a prediction for each
Answer questions 1 and 2: a text filter and a date range
Answer questions 3 and 4: a sorted top ten and a line value
Compare each result with your prediction and save the part file

lab.stretch: Rewrite question 2 with a half-open date range and explain why it is safer than BETWEEN

days.subtitle: What a row means before any query is written

days.title: One table, then two

sessions.title: CASE expressions and set operations
sessions.summary: CASE turns rules into columns; UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT combine whole result sets
outcomes: Write a CASE expression that sorts rows into bands
Count by condition with CASE inside an aggregate
Combine two result sets with UNION, INTERSECT or EXCEPT

lab.title: Questions 5 to 7: bands and sets
lab.summary: Predict, then answer three business questions with CASE bands, conditional counts and a set operation; save them to your answer file

steps.text: Write a prediction for each of the three questions
Question 5: order lines in quantity bands
Question 6: paid and free delivery per order status
Question 7: January customers who did not order in June
Save the part file

lab.stretch: Answer question 7 again with NOT EXISTS and confirm both give the same count

sessions.title: NULL and three-valued logic
sessions.summary: NULL is unknown, not zero or empty: comparisons with it are neither true nor false
outcomes: Predict the rows a comparison with NULL keeps
Use IS NULL, COALESCE and IS DISTINCT FROM on purpose
Explain why NOT IN with a NULL returns no rows

lab.title: Predict, then run: twelve NULL comparisons
lab.summary: With the assistant off, predict the row count of twelve short queries on the printed mini tables, run them, mark each prediction and repair the ones that did not say what was meant

steps.text: Print the mini customers and order lines
Predict the row count of each of the twelve queries on paper
Run the twelve and mark each prediction
Rewrite three queries so they say what was meant
Write the NULL rule you will keep

lab.stretch: Show NOT IN returning no rows when the list holds a NULL, and the NOT EXISTS that does not

sessions.title: Grouping and having
sessions.summary: GROUP BY changes the grain of the result; HAVING filters groups after they are formed
outcomes: Predict the number of rows a GROUP BY returns
Choose between WHERE and HAVING for a condition
Count distinct values inside a group

lab.title: Questions 8 to 11: groups
lab.summary: Predict, then answer four grouping questions: orders per store, busy customers, months and best-selling products; save them to your answer file

steps.text: Write a prediction for each of the four questions
Question 8: delivered orders per store
Question 9: customers with many orders, using HAVING
Question 10: orders and distinct customers per month
Question 11: products on many order lines
Save the part file

lab.stretch: Explain why COUNT(discount) and COUNT(*) differ on the order lines

sessions.title: Inner, outer, semi and anti joins
sessions.summary: Which rows survive a join, and how to ask for rows that have, or lack, a partner
outcomes: Predict the rows an inner and a left join return on small tables
Find rows without a partner with an anti join
Keep rows that have a partner without multiplying them, with a semi join

lab.title: Questions 12 to 15: joins
lab.summary: Predict, then answer four questions, one for each kind of join; save them to your answer file

steps.text: Write a prediction for each of the four questions
Question 12: delivered orders per store region
Question 13: customers and never-ordered customers per region
Question 14: active products that were never sold

lab.stretch: Write question 13 with a left join and with NOT EXISTS, and say which one a reader understands first

days.subtitle: Conditions, NULL, groups and the four kinds of join

days.title: Combining safely, then windows

sessions.title: Join fan-out and double counting
sessions.summary: A join to a many side repeats the rows of the one side, and every sum over them grows
outcomes: Detect fan-out by counting rows before and after a join
Aggregate to the right grain before joining
Explain a wrong total from the grain of each table it joined

lab.title: Questions 16 and 17: count once
lab.summary: See a sum grow when order lines meet delivery attempts, then answer two questions that need lines and attempts together without double counting; save them to your answer file

steps.text: Count rows before and after joining delivery attempts
Write a prediction for each of the two questions
Question 16: line value of orders that needed a second attempt
Question 17: orders and attempts per store in one result
Save the part file

lab.stretch: Find the share by which the naive sum of line values overstates the true one

sessions.title: Subqueries and common table expressions
sessions.summary: Build an answer in named steps, each of which you can run and check on its own
outcomes: Use a subquery in WHERE and in FROM
Write a query as a chain of common table expressions

lab.title: Questions 18 to 20, and the checker
lab.summary: Predict, then answer the last three questions in steps, one of them by the finance rule; then run the automatic checker over all twenty

steps.text: Write a prediction for each of the three questions
Question 18: products above their category's average price
Question 19: net revenue by month of delivery, by the finance rule
Question 20: the five customers with the highest net revenue

lab.stretch: Rewrite question 19 as one query without common table expressions and compare how easy each is to check

sessions.title: Partitions, ranking, lag and lead

outcomes: Write a window with a partition and an ordering
Choose between ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK at ties

lab.title: Window drills 1: top items per region

sessions.title: Running and moving aggregates
sessions.summary: Running totals, week-on-week change and seven-day averages, and the frame that decides them
outcomes: Compute a running total that restarts in each partition
Compute a week-on-week change with LAG over weekly totals
Choose a ROWS or a RANGE frame when days are missing

lab.title: Window drills 2: weeks and seven days
lab.summary: From the daily order table, compute week-on-week change per store, a running total within each month and seven-day averages that stay right across closed days; run the window checker

steps.text: Drill 4: weekly orders per store and the change from the week before
Drill 5: running net sales per store within each month
Drill 6: seven-day average net sales, ROWS against RANGE

lab.stretch: Fill the closed days with zero rows from a calendar and compare the three seven-day averages

days.title: Building and checking

sessions.title: Loading into constrained tables, and transactions
sessions.summary: Stage the raw file, sort out what the constraints would refuse, load the rest in one transaction, account for every row
outcomes: Write table definitions with keys, foreign keys and checks
Load a raw file through a staging table and record each rejected row with its reason
Group inserts, updates and deletes in a transaction and roll back on a failed check

Load the three extracts into all-text staging tables

sessions.title: Views that limit what is exposed

lab.title: Label the tables and build the analyst view
lab.summary: Mark the personal-data columns, label each table under the company's rule, and build a view the analysts can query without names, phones or e-mail

steps.text: Open the supplied July database
Mark each customer column: direct identifier, indirect identifier or neither

lab.stretch: Write a second view for the delivery team and list what it needs that the analysts do not

sessions.title: Query plans and indexes
sessions.summary: EXPLAIN shows how the engine will run a query; an index changes a lookup, rarely a scan of everything
outcomes: Read the operators of a query plan from the bottom up
Find where a filter is applied in a plan
Predict when an index changes a plan and when it does not

lab.title: Read two plans and watch an index change one
lab.summary: Read a join plan in DuckDB, then watch an index turn a scan into a search in SQLite; plan shapes only, no timings

steps.text: Read the plan of a join and group query
Find where the filter is applied

Run the ten queries through the tests

days.title: Capstone: the business orders brief
days.subtitle: For each participant: five minutes of live adaptation of one query, then two of questions on the assumptions note

capstone.summary: A ten-question stakeholder brief on a new synthetic dataset, answered in a repository of tested SQL with a note on assumptions, plus a timed AI-off check and a live adaptation of one query to a changed question
capstone.submission: Individual. A public GitHub repository link holding the answers to the ten questions of the business orders brief (labs/capstone/): one SQL file per question with a comment on its grain, a pytest test per question against a hand-checked fixture, the assumptions note and the log of any generated SQL and how it was checked, with the history kept. On the capstone day: the timed AI-off check, then five minutes of live adaptation of one query to a changed question and two minutes of questions on the assumptions note.

rubric.criterion: Correct answers: the ten queries return the trainer's key on the full business orders data
Tests: each query has a pytest test against a small fixture whose expected rows were worked out by hand, and the tests pass
Grain: each query states the grain of its result and of every table it joins, and no total is counted twice
Assumptions note: every business rule of the brief stated, applied and traced to the query that uses it
Verification log: every query an assistant wrote or changed is recorded with the test that caught or passed it
Minimal exposure: no answer returns a personal-data column the question does not need
